newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission says basmati abatement is safe.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission says basmati abatement is safe.

text.p: Indian basmati rice exporters will not lose rights to a 250 ecu per tonne tariff cut on European Union imports under a new tariff agreement with the United States, an EU Commission official said on Tuesday.

"There is no question of Indian basmati rice exporters losing their 250 ecus tarif abatement on rice shipments to the EU," the official said, commenting on a statement from the All India Rice Exporters' Association.

Fears that the abatement might be lost came as the EU and US neared agreement on a cumulative tariff recovery system for transatlantic rice imports which allows exporters to reclaim accumulated overpayments.
"What appears to have given rise to fears is the prospect of tighter controls on quality and price which will be part of the new agreement.
"The EU will have to strengthen controls but the flat rate abatement for basmati will remain unless exporters themselves wish to change," the official said.
Under the basmati rice tariff arrangements, Indian exporters get a flat rate cut of 250 ecus per tonne on the tariff rate which the Commission said is currently 260 ecus per tonne.
The abatement was awarded to Indian exporters because of the high price of basmati which ranges from 600 to 800 dollars a tonne.
The EU imports between 60,000 and 80,000 tonnes of basmati annually and the official confirmed that the figure is rising due to consumer demand.
In New Delhi, Indian rice exporters said they would lose about 70 percent of their Basmati exports to the European Union if the new EU regulation was approved.
"The move will reduce exports of Basmati rice to the EU from India by over 70 percent in one year," said R.S. Seshadri, a senior official of the All India Rice Exporters Association.
Seshadri said EU authorities had prepared a draft regulation and sought the views of rice exporting countries before it was put to the vote on February 20 in Brussels.
According to the draft import regime, the quality of imports would need to be verified based on factors like aroma, the milling yield and the percentage of brokens, he said.
AIREA said all imported rice would attract full duty and the duty on Indian exports would rise sharply.
If the new regulation were applied the existing concession of 250 Ecus for Indian Basmati could be claimed only after detailed data were provided on the price and quality of each consignment.

"As Indian Basmati rice is the costliest rice, we are going to be affected very badly by this new system and the importers and exporters may feel shy of locking up a huge amount of money to be claimed after a span of 6-12 months," the AIREA said in a statement.
Seshadri said Indian exporters were paying a duty of $18 per tonne on Indian Basmati rice and this would shoot up to $268 once the legislation was passed.
"The EU must be left in no doubt that if this was done then India would take it up at the WTO (World Trade Organisation)," Seshadri said.
The AIREA said it had asked the Indian government to take up the matter, and the Commerce Ministry had told Indian envoys in EU countries of its views.
